title: IRIS: Integrated Reliability Imaging System
oneLiner: A five-camera inspection station designed to photograph every returned fuel cell column before teardown destroys the evidence of its field condition. I designed and built it, then handed it off to operations; the resolution, framing and coverage numbers here are the design targets it was built to hit.
cardSummary: Five-camera station that photographs returned fuel cell columns before teardown
whatIOwnedSummary: I owned all of it. I set the optical specification and coverage geometry, designed the mechanics and registration scheme, built the capture software and operator console, ran procurement and vendor selection, traced the network fault, and wrote the handoff documentation set.

path.decision: Took sample photos of returned columns, which Reliability confirmed showed what they needed, then measured the plate thickness in pixels on those samples to work out the resolution the station required.

path.why: Reliability wanted every face captured (front, back, and sides) and Operations wanted as little delay as possible; the front face is the most accessible and carries the most critical information.

path.decision: Translated the 0.1 mm requirement into a 53 µm/px design target, using a 5 MP sensor, 35 mm lens, and a ±13 mm depth-of-field standoff window.
Chose five fixed cameras over one motorized camera.
path.why: Captures the column in one shot with no added time per unit, no drift, and no single point of failure.

path.decision: Handled dust and tint with controlled lighting and a color card in frame; designed the registration to hold framing within ±2.9 mm without touching production tooling.
Built the capture app with automated focus and exposure checks and per-unit override logs; verified gap-free five-camera coverage by script and tracked open items in the V&V record.
Traced a camera-discovery failure to a single corporate firewall rule and delivered the exception package and commissioning runbook.
path.why: The fix needed a centrally applied exception under IT security review, and someone else would commission the station after my internship.

claims.title: Derived the optical spec at 53 µm/px from a 0.1 mm feature-resolution requirement
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Resolve roughly 0.1 mm of surface change across the full column face. Reliable detection needs about two pixels across the smallest feature, so one pixel cannot straddle an edge and average it away.
claims.method: Worked backwards from the requirement rather than from available hardware. The sampling rule set the required scale; frame width is fixed by the part, so dividing it across the sensor's pixel count gave the achievable scale. Aperture was then chosen for depth of field rather than brightness.
claims.resultMetric: The chain fixed sensor, lens, and working distance, and produced a ±13 mm standoff window that became the tolerance the mechanical design had to fit inside. Every later optical decision traces back to two inputs: the feature size and the frame width.
claims.limitations:
A design value computed from component specifications and frame geometry, never confirmed against a captured image.
Image a calibration target at the working distance and measure the actual field of view to confirm the achieved scale.

claims.title: Chose five fixed cameras by scripted layout comparison and verified gap-free coverage
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Every region of the outward face imaged head-on with no gaps, despite protruding features that shadow the regions Reliability cares about most. Had to fit within teardown takt time.
claims.method: Generated candidate layouts by script rather than laying them out by hand, and compared coverage for a single camera, for cameras centered on the protrusions, and for cameras with the protrusions at frame boundaries. Also evaluated a single camera on a motorized vertical stage.
claims.resultMetric: Boundary placement moves the hardest regions to mid-frame, where lighting and resolution are best, with overlap at every seam. Centering on the protrusions is the intuitive approach and leaves those regions shadowed. The motorized single-camera option was rejected on cycle time and on drift, since a moving stage on a dusty floor is both a repeatability risk and a single point of failure.
claims.limitations:
Coverage confirmed in geometry only, never checked against a physical column with cameras mounted.
Confirm the layout holds across column variants with differing module counts.

claims.title: Designed the registration to hold framing within ±2.9 mm with no contact to production tooling
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Framing had to stay inside the ±13 mm standoff window set by the optics, across carts that vary unit to unit, without adding fixturing or slowing teardown.
claims.method: Since a station that touches production tooling risks being shifted or damaged in daily use, I designed the registration to be entirely workpiece-referenced. Vertical position comes from a live-view band on a self-locking crank, depth from a projected laser gap cue, and rotation is set by eye to a band. I measured position variation across production carts and stacked the contributions into a worst-case framing budget.
claims.resultMetric: Roughly four times margin inside the optical standoff window. The cart is never clamped, docked, or modified, so teardown flow is unchanged and the station can be relocated without recalibration.
claims.limitations:
A budget computed from measured cart variation, not a spread measured with the station operating on the line. By-eye rotation was not characterized across multiple operators before handoff.
Have several operators each position the same unit and measure the spread, to confirm the by-eye references hold across people rather than one person.

claims.title: Built the capture software end to end, gating every image on focus and exposure
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Cannot slow teardown, roughly one minute per unit. Has to work on an operator's first shift given high technician turnover, so the system must catch bad images rather than depend on anyone noticing them. Any override has to remain traceable.
claims.method: One pedal press fires all cameras simultaneously. Each image is scored for sharpness and exposure before acceptance; a failure flags that specific camera for individual re-fire rather than costing the whole capture. Overrides are written into the unit record alongside the image.
claims.resultMetric: A full unit runs from serial entry to completion in a browser, with per-camera retake. Every stored image carries its focus and exposure verdicts and any override flag, so the archive stays honest about which frames a human waved through.
claims.limitations:
Gate thresholds shipped as placeholders; the calibration tool exists, but calibration against real captures had not been done at handoff. Verified against simulated and USB cameras only, never production cameras.
Time a full unit against takt with a real operator, which is the constraint the design was built around and the most important thing never measured.

claims.title: Made camera count configuration-driven and handed off a full commissioning package
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Someone else would commission and own the station after my internship. A two-column expansion considered as a potential upgrade to reduce takt time. Vendor software versions change, so anything version-specific would go stale.
claims.method: Moved camera count, backend selection, and network tuning into a configuration file, and built three interchangeable camera backends covering production hardware, any USB camera, and a hardware-free simulator. Wrote a readiness script that tests the actual constraint rather than assuming a software version.
claims.resultMetric: End-to-end runs verified at one, two, and five cameras, so the two-column expansion to ten cameras should need no software changes. Testing stopped at five cameras. The handoff was seven documents: a handoff memo with status and ownership, a commissioning runbook, the firewall exception package for IT, a decision log of 19 locked design choices, a verification record with 13 open items (each naming the event that closes it), a code guide written for a non-programmer working with an AI assistant, and an asset inventory.
claims.limitations:
The handoff had not been exercised when I left. Nobody had brought the station up using only the documentation, so gaps in it are unknown.
Have the new owner do a dry run from the runbook alone and record every point where they get stuck.

outcome: Built and handed off to operations eight weeks after the project started. The capture software runs end to end: a full unit goes from serial entry to a focus- and exposure-gated capture in a browser, verified at one, two, and five cameras on simulated and USB camera backends. Commissioning on the line was blocked by a corporate firewall rule on the managed station PC that stopped camera discovery. I traced it to the specific rule and delivered an exception package and runbook before handoff, so the resolution, framing and coverage figures above remain design targets rather than measurements from the line.

interfaces.notes: One cable per camera carries both power and data. Expansion to ten cameras is additional ports rather than a topology change.

GigE Vision on an isolated subnet with no gateway and no route to the corporate network. Corporate connectivity uses a separate adapter on the same machine. This is the boundary where discovery failed.
Single keystroke triggers a capture, so the operator's hands stay on the cart. Deliberately the only physical input in the workflow.
Images written under the unit serial, each carrying its focus and exposure verdicts and any operator override. This is the record of what happened, not just the pictures.
Serial-to-image linkage defined as the next integration step. Images are serial-tagged on the station in the interim, so nothing is lost if the integration lands later.
No physical contact, by design. A station that touches production tooling risks being shifted or damaged in daily use, so all registration is workpiece-referenced.

evidence.label: Showcase poster
evidence.note: Intern showcase poster, August 2026: requirements, optical derivation chain, five-camera coverage comparison, station CAD render, and the operator console.

evidence.label: Commissioning package
evidence.note: Seven documents: handoff memo, commissioning runbook, firewall exception package, decision log, verification record with open items, code guide, and asset inventory. Internal; not publicly released.

projectRisks: Commissioning was not completed before handoff. Camera discovery was blocked at handoff by a host firewall rule on the corporate-managed PC, and the fix needed a centrally applied exception under IT security review. I traced it to the specific rule and blocked process and delivered the exception package and runbook. Ticket ownership transferred to my manager before I left.

The production camera driver was never exercised against real hardware. I built simulator and USB camera backends to verify the full pipeline end to end, and a readiness script that isolates which layer is failing at bring-up.

Focus and exposure thresholds shipped as placeholders, since real values depend on real optics and lighting. The calibration tool and procedure are built and documented; the step takes about ten minutes once cameras are live.
Optical resolution and framing budget are design values, not measurements taken with the system running on the line. The framing budget was sized against measured variation across production carts.

Phase 1 images the outward face only, a scope decision to hit the timeline. The software should support the extension unmodified (tested to five cameras), so adding it is a fixturing problem rather than a redesign.

lessons.text: I was product owner, mechanical designer, software engineer, and network debugger at once, so every trade-off went through me. Choosing an aperture for depth of field was also choosing how precisely an operator would have to position a cart. Owning both ends made those couplings visible in a way a specialist role would not have.

Reliability and Operations each set constraints that shaped the design fundamentally. Reliability needing every region imaged is what drove the five-camera layout. I learned to find the binding constraint from each group early rather than designing and then seeking approval.

Lead times drove more decisions than any technical analysis. Component availability shaped the camera and lens selection, and the station PC not arriving on schedule forced the software to become host-agnostic. Treating procurement as an engineering input rather than an administrative step would have changed my sequencing from the start.

Designing the handoff early changed what I built. Knowing I would not be the one commissioning the station is why camera count is set in a configuration file (as opposed to being hard-coded), and why the readiness check prints fixes rather than error codes.

IT was the stakeholder I did not think to consult. Reliability and Operations were obvious sources of requirements; the corporate network was infrastructure I assumed would just work. It became the binding constraint. On any project touching managed IT systems, I would have a meeting with them outlining the requirements of the project in week one.
